lessons.title: The records an abattoir must keep
lessons.html:
Administration supports compliance

Good administration keeps the abattoir legal, traceable and well managed. Under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and its regulations, and under other laws, the abattoir must be able to show records to inspectors and auditors. A foreman is responsible for making sure the records from the production floor are complete, accurate and filed.

Main record groups

GroupExamples
Livestock receivingMovement documents, owner details, brand or tag numbers, number and species, arrival time, lairage pen
SlaughterDaily slaughter register, carcass numbers linked to owners, carcass mass, classification
InspectionAnte-mortem and post-mortem findings, detentions, condemnations
HygienePre-operational checks, cleaning records, water test results, pest control, microbiological results
TemperatureChiller logs, steriliser checks, dispatch temperatures
Condemned materialQuantities, storage, disposal and collection slips
DispatchDelivery notes, customer, vehicle, carcass numbers
PeopleTime and attendance, leave, training records, medical fitness, disciplinary records
SafetyIncident and injury reports, equipment inspections, first aid register
MaintenanceBreakdowns, repairs, calibration of scales and thermometers

Traceability

Traceability means being able to follow a carcass back to the animal and its owner, and forward to the customer. It depends on linking records at every step: movement document, lairage pen, slaughter number, carcass label and delivery note. If a residue or disease problem is found, traceability allows a quick, targeted recall.

lessons.title: Good administrative practice
lessons.html:
Making records reliable

  • Standard forms: use the approved, version-controlled forms so everyone records the same information.
  • Complete at the time: records are filled in when the activity happens.
  • Legible and permanent: pen, not pencil; no correction fluid; corrections crossed out once and initialled.
  • Signed and checked: the person doing the task signs, and the supervisor verifies.
  • Filed systematically: by date and record type, in a place where they are protected from water, pests and loss.
  • Kept for the required period: follow the retention period in your procedures and legal requirements.

Electronic systems

Many abattoirs use software for weighing, labelling, classification and stock control. Electronic records must be backed up, and access must be controlled with personal passwords. Never share passwords; records must show who did what.

Document control

Procedures and forms change over time. Document control makes sure that only the current version is in use on the floor. Each document has a number, version and date. Old versions are removed from work areas and archived.

Personal information

Worker records contain personal information such as ID numbers, addresses, medical details and disciplinary history. Keep them confidential and locked away, and share them only with people who need them for their work. The Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 sets rules for how personal information is handled.

Communication paperwork

Shift handover reports, meeting minutes, memos and notices are also part of administration. A good handover report states slaughter numbers, problems, outstanding actions and anything the next shift must know, such as a chiller that is running warm.

lessons.title: Human resource and stock administration
lessons.html:
People administration

Accurate people records protect both the worker and the employer.

  • Time and attendance: clock cards or biometric systems. Check them daily and approve overtime correctly, in line with the Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997.
  • Leave: record annual, sick and family responsibility leave. Require medical certificates where company policy and the law allow.
  • Training records: who was trained on what, when and by whom. Auditors check that workers are trained in hygiene and safety.
  • Medical fitness: many abattoirs require medical checks for food handlers.
  • Discipline: keep warnings and hearing records according to the disciplinary code.

Stock and consumables

Administration also controls the materials the floor uses: protective clothing, knives, chemicals, packaging, labels and spares.

  • Use requisition forms or the stock system to issue items.
  • Keep minimum stock levels and reorder in time so production never stops for lack of supplies.
  • Record issues per section and compare with budget.
  • Count stock regularly and investigate losses.
  • Control inspection stamps, classification rollers and condemned material keys with a sign-out register.

Reports to management

The foreman compiles daily or weekly reports: animals received and slaughtered, yield, condemnations, downtime and its causes, incidents, absenteeism and overtime. Reports should be short, factual and show trends. Management uses them to make decisions, so accuracy matters.

Key points

  • Records cover livestock, slaughter, inspection, hygiene, temperature, condemned material, dispatch, people, safety and maintenance.
  • Traceability links each carcass to its owner and its customer.
  • Records must be completed at the time, legible, signed, filed and kept for the required period.
  • Use only the current version of each procedure and form.
  • Keep personal information confidential.
  • Control consumables, stamps and keys with registers.
